newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik leader heads for peace talks in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Tajik leader heads for peace talks in Afghanistan.

text.p: Tajikistan President Imomali Rakhmonov left on Tuesday for peace talks with Islamist rebel leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri in northern Afghanistan as further violence rocked the former Soviet republic.
Airport officials in the Tajik capital Dushanbe confirmed Rakhmonov's departure for Afghanistan early on Tuesday.
The Tajik Interior Ministry said one government soldier was killed and another wounded in a shootout with opposition guerrillas near Dushanbe late on Monday.
"We carried out a raid on a suspected opposition base in Dzhangalabad when the shooting occurred," said a ministry spokesman.
A guerrilla comander was killed in the raid and three opposition fighters were captured, he added.
Nuri arrived in the Afghan town of Kunduz on Monday for the peace talks after his aircraft was delayed by Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia, the United Nations said.
The talks were expected to begin when Rakhmonov and U.N. special envoy Gerd Merrem arrive in Kunduz.
Nuri was travelling to the talks in a U.N. aircraft on Saturday when warplanes belonging to the Taleban forced it to land.
The Taleban said on Sunday the aircraft had been released and authorised to continue its flight.
U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said there was an apparent misunderstanding between the United Nations and the Taleban.
Fighting has increased in Tajikistan since the peace talks were announced at the end of last month, with each side trying to strengthen its hand at the negotiating table.
There have also been a spate of attacks against Russian servicemen based in Tajikistan, who help prop up Rakhmonov's administration. The opposition is widely held to have been responsible.

Tens of thousands have been killed and many more made homeless in the four-year civil war in the mountainous country bordering Afghanistan and China. Regional and clan rivalries underlie the conflict between the Islamist rebels and the secular government.
